sectors.label: Group Contrasts
sectors.goal: Test differences between groups — parametric (ANOVA family) when assumptions hold, non-parametric (Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis, Wilcoxon, Friedman) when they do not.
sectors.description: Umbrella for inferential group comparison. Parametric ANOVA decomposes variance under normality and homoscedasticity; when those assumptions fail, rank-based or permutation alternatives (Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis, Wilcoxon, Friedman) deliver robust contrasts. The default lens for experimental and quasi-experimental entrepreneurship studies — programme evaluations, treatment comparisons, A/B tests.
hypotheses: H0: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ (no mean differences across treatment groups).
H1: at least one programme mean differs in entrepreneurial intention / self-efficacy / new-venture creation rate.
Interaction: the effect of an incubation programme depends on the entrepreneur's prior experience (factorial design).
conditions: You have ≥3 discrete groups (or 2 groups + a covariate → ANCOVA).
The outcome is metric / continuous (intention scale, growth %, weekly revenue).
You manipulate or sample factor levels rather than relying on observational covariates.
You can defend independence, near-normal residuals, and homogeneity of variance — or use the Welch / robust variants.
procedure: Define factors and levels theoretically before collecting data.
Run Levene's test for variance homogeneity; switch to Welch's F if violated.
Inspect residual plots; transform or use rank-based ANOVA when normality fails.
Run the omnibus F; if significant, follow up with Tukey HSD or Bonferroni post-hoc.
Report effect sizes (η², ω², partial η²) in addition to p-values (Lakens, 2013).

authors.why: Effect-size practical primer cited 8,100+ times.

authors.why: Monte Carlo evidence on robustness of F under non-normality — vital for small entrepreneurship samples.

authors.name: Olejnik & Algina

sectors.label: Regression / GLM
sectors.goal: Test a pre-specified theoretical model with interpretable coefficients and inference on individual predictors.
sectors.description: The interpretable workhorse. Logistic regression remains the standard reference model for binary entrepreneurship outcomes — survival, intention, market entry — because its coefficients translate to odds ratios that stakeholders can read.
hypotheses: H1: prior entrepreneurial exposure raises the log-odds of new-venture entry, controlling for age, gender, education.
H2: each unit of perceived self-efficacy multiplies the odds of intention to start a business by exp(β).
H3: financing constraints negatively moderate the effect of opportunity recognition on venture survival.
conditions: The outcome is binary, count, continuous or time-to-event and you have a theoretically defensible specification.
N ≥ 10–15 events per predictor (Osborne, 2014) for stable logistic estimates.
You want interpretable parameters with confidence intervals, p-values and odds-ratios.
Functional form is plausibly linear (in the link function) after transformation.
procedure: Specify the model from theory; pre-register interactions if possible.
Check VIFs and condition indices; drop or combine collinear predictors.
Fit the GLM with the appropriate link (logit, probit, log, identity).
Report coefficients, ORs, 95% CIs, AUROC and Pseudo-R² (logistic) or adjusted R² (OLS).
Run residual diagnostics, influence plots and out-of-sample validation on a hold-out.
software: R: lm, glm, lme4, survival, glmnet

sectors.label: PLS-SEM
sectors.goal: Estimate complex path models with latent constructs (entrepreneurial orientation, self-efficacy, opportunity recognition) when prediction matters and theory is exploratory.
sectors.description: Partial least squares structural equation modelling. Dominant in entrepreneurship and management when constructs are latent, formative or reflective, and the goal is to maximise explained variance in endogenous targets — not to confirm a strict covariance structure.
hypotheses: H1: entrepreneurial orientation → firm performance is mediated by innovation capability.
H2: the path from perceived behavioural control to intention is moderated by gender (multi-group analysis).
H3: a higher-order "dynamic capabilities" construct predicts venture growth above its first-order dimensions.
conditions: You have multiple latent constructs measured by reflective (or formative) indicators.
Sample size meets the inverse-square-root or 10× rule (≥ 10 indicators on the most complex construct).
The literature is exploratory or aims at prediction — you would not run covariance-based SEM.
You want to evaluate a measurement model and a structural model jointly.
assumes: Reflective indicators load > 0.70 on their construct
procedure: Step 1 — Measurement model: indicator reliability, composite reliability, AVE, HTMT.
Step 2 — Structural model: inner VIF, path coefficients with bootstrap CIs, R², f², Q².
Run PLSpredict to assess out-of-sample relevance vs. linear benchmark.
For multi-group hypotheses, conduct PLS-MGA with permutation tests.
Report Hair et al. (2022) checklist explicitly in the methods section.

authors.why: Cited 240,000+ times — universal rules-of-thumb for multivariate work.

sectors.label: fsQCA
sectors.goal: Identify combinations of conditions that are sufficient (and/or necessary) for the outcome — recipes, not net effects.
sectors.description: Set-theoretic, configurational method built on Boolean algebra and fuzzy sets. Embraces equifinality (multiple paths to success), conjunctural causation (variables interact in bundles), and asymmetry (the conditions for success differ from those for failure).
hypotheses: H1: high entrepreneurial passion AND high self-efficacy AND tolerance of risk are jointly sufficient for an effectual logic.
H2: institutional support is a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for high-growth ventures.
H3: the recipe for opportunity exploitation in low-support contexts differs from the recipe in well-funded ecosystems (asymmetry).
conditions: Small-to-medium N (typically 10–150 cases) where regression would be unstable.
You expect multiple equally valid pathways to the same outcome.
Theory suggests bundles of conditions matter more than isolated effects.
You can calibrate sets from theoretical anchors, not just data quantiles.
assumes: Negation of the outcome analysed separately
procedure: Calibrate raw scores into fuzzy membership using three anchors (full-in, crossover, full-out).
Run necessity analysis on each condition and its negation; report consistency and coverage.
Build the truth table; set frequency cutoff (≥ 1 for small-N, higher for larger samples) and consistency threshold (≥ 0.80).
Generate parsimonious, intermediate and complex solutions; report the intermediate as primary.
Robustness checks: vary calibration anchors and consistency thresholds; document any case re-classification.

sectors.label: Clustering
sectors.goal: Discover latent groups, types or trajectories without a labelled outcome — entrepreneur archetypes, ecosystem typologies, growth-pattern segments.
sectors.description: Unsupervised learning that partitions cases by similarity. The default method for building data-driven typologies of entrepreneurs, startups or ecosystems when you do not yet have a target variable.
hypotheses: H1: there exist k distinct entrepreneur profiles characterised by combinations of motivation, education and risk-tolerance.
H2: sustainable startups cluster into archetypes that map to differentiated policy needs.
H3: the optimal partition (BIC / silhouette) is stable across split-half replications.
conditions: No labelled outcome — you need to *find* groups, not predict them.
You can defend the distance metric and feature scaling.
Theory or domain knowledge can later interpret and name the clusters.
You commit to validating stability (split-half, bootstrap, gap statistic).
assumes: Comparable feature scales (z-scoring or robust scaling)
Latent group structure exists in feature space
procedure: Theory-driven variable selection — Ketchen & Shook warn against irrelevant variables that "fog" the structure.
Standardise features; consider Mahalanobis or Gower for mixed types.
Run hierarchical (Ward) for visual exploration via dendrogram, then k-means on the chosen k.
Validate using silhouette, gap statistic, BIC (for GMM), and split-half replication.
Profile clusters with ANOVA / chi-square contrasts; name them theoretically.

sectors.label: Boosted Trees
sectors.goal: Predict accurately on tabular entrepreneurship data — survival, funding, exit, market entry — usually the strong baseline that beats logistic regression.
sectors.description: Tree-based ensembles excel on the tabular data that dominate entrepreneurship: GEM micro-files, firmographic panels, survey-plus-register linkages. Random Forest gives robust importance scores; XGBoost / LightGBM typically win on raw accuracy.
hypotheses: H1: boosted trees outperform logistic regression in AUROC for predicting venture entry on GEM cross-country data.
H2: the most predictive variables for first-year survival differ from those that classical theory emphasises.
H3: SHAP interaction values reveal a non-linear effect of self-efficacy that scales with prior exposure.
conditions: Tabular data with mixed predictors and meaningful class signal.
N sufficient for splits (rule of thumb: ≥ 200 events for stable Random Forest).
Prediction is a deliverable — for policy targeting, screening, scouting.
Discipline of train / validation / test split is non-negotiable.
assumes: No leakage between feature engineering and resampling
procedure: Stratified train/validation/test split (commonly 70/15/15) with fixed seed.
Tune hyperparameters with k-fold CV on the training set; never touch the test set.
Compare against logistic baseline; report ΔAUROC with DeLong test.
Report feature importance (gain / permutation) and SHAP attributions on the test set.
Calibrate predicted probabilities (Platt / isotonic) before policy use.

sectors.label: Explainable AI / EBM
sectors.goal: Use predictive models as a microscope to surface non-linear effects and conditional interactions that feed back into theory.
sectors.description: A bridge between prediction and explanation. EBM and SHAP give you globally faithful, interpretable attributions — ideal for entrepreneurship studies that want both accuracy and theoretical contribution.
hypotheses: H1: a SHAP analysis identifies a non-linear effect of perceived feasibility above a threshold that classical theory missed.
H2: an EBM reveals a stable interaction between gender and risk-tolerance that holds across resamples.
H3: Friedman's H detects global interaction strength > 0.10 between context and individual variables.
conditions: You have a strong predictive model and want to derive theoretical insights from it.
Stakeholders need explanations, not only predictions.
Interactions matter substantively (not just incidentally).
You can build a stable background distribution for SHAP attributions.
procedure: Train the strongest predictive model (XGBoost, NN) and a transparent EBM in parallel.
Build a stratified background sample (e.g. 100 cases) for SHAP.
Report mean |SHAP| and SHAP interaction values; show stability across seeds.
Use ALE plots for marginal shape, ICE for individual heterogeneity.
Quantify global interaction strength with Friedman's H.

sectors.label: Neural Network
sectors.goal: Predict on high-dimensional, unstructured or richly interactive data — pitch-deck text, founder voices, social-media images, platform traces.
sectors.description: Deep neural networks shine where the input is unstructured (text, images, sequences) or where conditional high-order interactions matter. In entrepreneurship: predicting funding rounds from pitch text, classifying founder narratives, forecasting platform-mediated venture survival.
hypotheses: H1: a fine-tuned BERT classifier on pitch-deck text predicts seed-funding outcomes with AUROC > 0.85.
H2: a multimodal model that combines founder voice features with firmographics outperforms either modality alone.
H3: an autoencoder reveals a low-dimensional manifold of entrepreneurial trajectories.
conditions: Your inputs are unstructured (text, image, audio, sequence) or extremely high-dimensional.
You have ≥ a few thousand labelled examples (or pretrained backbones to fine-tune).
You can afford GPU compute and the engineering discipline DL demands.
Accuracy outweighs full interpretability — pair with XAI for insight.
assumes: Reproducibility seeds, environments and configs versioned
procedure: Curate the data; verify train/val/test partitions are leakage-free.
Choose architecture by modality: MLP for tabular, CNN for images, transformer for text/sequence.
Use early stopping on validation; track learning curves to detect overfitting.
Compare against a strong tabular baseline (XGBoost) and against a transparent model (logistic).
Pair with SHAP / DeepSHAP / attention visualisation for partial interpretability.
software: NVIDIA / Colab / local Ollama for LLMs

rings.label: Data structure
rings.sub: What does your dataset look like?

questions.text: What is the core analytic goal of your study?
questions.hint: Pick the framing that best matches the central purpose of the research question.

options.label: Test a pre-specified theoretical model with interpretable parameters
Estimate paths between latent constructs (e.g. entrepreneurial orientation, self-efficacy)
Identify equifinal configurations / sufficient conditions ("recipes for success")
Maximise out-of-sample prediction accuracy on new cases
Discover non-linear effects & interactions to feed back into theory
Build typologies / discover latent groups (no labelled outcome)
Compare means across experimental or treatment groups

questions.text: What is the type of the outcome variable?

options.label: Binary (yes/no) — survival, intention, market entry
Continuous (revenue growth, scale score, performance index)
Count (number of opportunities, patents, fundraising rounds)
Time-to-event (hazard of failure, duration to first sale)
Multiple endogenous latent constructs (path model)
Set membership — degree of belonging to a fuzzy outcome
No outcome variable — exploratory / unsupervised

questions.text: Are your key constructs latent (unobservable) or directly measured?
questions.hint: Latent constructs (e.g. perceived self-efficacy) are estimated from multi-item scales and need a measurement model.

options.label: Multiple latent constructs with reflective multi-item scales
A few latent constructs already aggregated into composite scores
All directly observed / register / firmographic variables
Mix of observed variables and unstructured data (text, image)

questions.text: How is causality conceptualised in your theory?
questions.hint: fsQCA assumes asymmetry and equifinality; regression / PLS-SEM assume symmetric net effects.

options.label: Symmetric net effects — each predictor adds (or multiplies) independently
Configurational — outcomes arise from bundles of conditions
Asymmetric — the recipe for success differs from that for failure
Unknown / driven by data — let the algorithm decide

questions.text: What is the sample size relative to the number of predictors / conditions?
questions.hint: Rough order of magnitude is fine.

options.label: Very small N (< 50) — case-oriented research
Small to moderate N (50–300), few predictors
Moderate N (300–2,000), many predictors
Large N (2,000–50,000), tabular data
Very large N (> 50,000) or rich item-level data

questions.text: What is the dominant nature of your predictors / inputs?

options.label: All categorical — factorial / experimental design
All continuous — composite indices, financial ratios
Mixed tabular (categorical + continuous + counts)
Multi-item Likert scales tapping latent constructs
Unstructured (text, images, sequences, social-media)

questions.text: How linear are the relationships you expect?

options.label: Linear or monotone after standard transformations
Mildly non-linear with a few interactions
Strongly non-linear, high-order conditional interactions
Configurational, not functional — bundles matter
Not applicable — exploratory / unsupervised

questions.text: Do you need a measurement model for your constructs, or are observed scores enough?
questions.hint: PLS-SEM only adds value if you must validate a measurement model with multiple indicators.

options.label: Yes — multiple multi-item constructs need measurement validation (loadings, AVE, HTMT)
I have validated scales already; observed composites are fine
No latent constructs at all — only observed variables

questions.text: Are your inputs tabular, or do they include unstructured signals (text, image, audio, sequence)?
questions.hint: XGBoost dominates tabular benchmarks; deep nets dominate unstructured ones.

options.label: Strictly tabular — rows and columns of mixed types
Tabular with embeddings or engineered features from text
Mostly unstructured (pitch text, founder voice, images)
A mix — multimodal model would add value

questions.text: Is the deliverable a prediction or a theory-relevant explanation?
questions.hint: Boosted trees are best when the score itself is the deliverable; XAI / EBM is best when the goal is to understand and theorise from the model.

options.label: A prediction score for screening or policy targeting
Both prediction AND interpretable feature interactions for the paper
Mostly explanation — I want to surface a non-linear effect for theory

questions.text: Can you justify set-membership calibration anchors from theory (full-in / cross-over / full-out)?
questions.hint: fsQCA only delivers if the calibration is theoretical, not data-driven quantiles.

options.label: Yes — anchors are anchored in theory or qualitative knowledge of cases
Partially — I would use percentile rules with theoretical sense-check
No — I cannot justify clean anchors; better to model functionally

questions.text: How will you validate the discovered clusters?
questions.hint: Reviewers expect at least one stability test plus a profiling analysis.

options.label: Internal validity (silhouette / gap / BIC) + split-half replication
Profile clusters with ANOVA / chi-square contrasts then name them theoretically
Use them as features for a downstream prediction model
Not sure yet — need guidance
One factor with ≥3 independent groups (one-way ANOVA)
Two or more factors crossed (factorial ANOVA, interactions of interest)
Repeated measures or mixed (within + between)
Two groups + a continuous covariate to control for (ANCOVA)
Multiple correlated outcomes (MANOVA)
Non-parametric: ranks (Mann–Whitney / Kruskal–Wallis / Wilcoxon)

questions.text: Do you have the labelled data and compute to support neural networks?
questions.hint: A few thousand labels and a GPU are usually the minimum; otherwise XGBoost wins.

options.label: Yes — thousands of labels + GPU access (or pretrained backbone to fine-tune)
I can use a pretrained model (BERT, ResNet) and fine-tune the head only
Limited labels — I should fall back to a strong tabular baseline

questions.text: Which variant of the regression family fits your outcome best?

options.label: Logistic regression (binary outcome, odds ratios)
OLS / linear regression (continuous outcome)
Poisson / Negative Binomial (count outcome)
Cox proportional hazards (time-to-event)
Multilevel / mixed-effects (nested data)

questions.text: You are between two equally plausible techniques. Which trade-off matters more?
questions.hint: If the leaderboard is genuinely tied, this is your steering wheel.

options.label: Interpretability of parameters and confidence intervals
Configurational logic — multiple paths to the outcome
Out-of-sample accuracy on a hold-out test set
Theoretical novelty surfaced by a strong predictive model
Ability to estimate latent constructs jointly
Discovery of types or trajectories in the data

questions.text: How important is interpretability of the model?
questions.hint: Who needs to understand the model, and at what level of detail?

options.label: Critical — non-technical stakeholders need to read parameters
Need feature importance + interaction shape
Useful — global feature importance is enough
Secondary — accuracy first
Not relevant — descriptive / exploratory

questions.text: What validation strategy will you commit to?

options.label: Hypothesis testing with p-values and confidence intervals
Bootstrap path significance + PLSpredict
Train / validation / test split with out-of-sample metrics
Truth-table consistency, coverage and robustness checks
Cluster stability — split-half / bootstrap / silhouette

questions.text: Will you triangulate with a complementary method?
questions.hint: Many strong entrepreneurship papers pair a primary method with a configurational or predictive complement.
